chunks: Why measure current. The question: Why do you want to measure current?
Current is the quantity that heats wires, makes motor torque and tells you how much battery charge has moved. Voltage alone often cannot show these things.

So products measure current for four jobs: protection (shut down on a short), control (regulate a power converter or motor), monitoring (battery charge and power) and diagnostics (spot a stalled motor or a broken wire).
The job decides how fast and how accurate the measurement must be.
Think of the water meter on a house. It spots a burst pipe because flow suddenly jumps (protection). It can tell a pump how hard to work (control).
It adds up the total for the bill (monitoring). And a flow of zero while a tap is open tells you something is blocked (diagnostics).
A burst pipe needs a fast alarm, but billing needs a precise total. The analogy leaves out the heat: in electronics, the flow itself causes damage by warming the pipes.
Four jobs for the same measurement.
Each job puts a different demand on the sensor: speed for protection, bandwidth and linearity for control, low offset for monitoring, moderate accuracy for diagnostics.
Overcurrent protection: shutting off when current exceeds a safe limit. Torque constant ( k t ): how much twisting force (newton-meters) a motor makes per amp.
Coulomb counting: adding up current over time to track battery charge. Stall current: the large current a motor draws when its shaft cannot turn.
Offset: a small constant error in the reading, which adds up when you integrate.
Short a 12 volts supply through 10 microhenries of wiring. The current rises at V over L equals 12 over 10 micro H equals 1.
2 amps per microsecond, so it reaches 12 amps after 10 microseconds. A trip circuit with a 1 microseconds delay catches it near 1 or 2 amps over the limit.
A slow check every 100 microseconds would let it reach about 120 amps. Now take battery tracking: a 10 milliamps offset on a 2 Ah cell is 0. 01 times 1 over 2 equals 0.
5 % of capacity per hour. That is the whole idea.
"Four reasons. Protection, because current is what overheats and destroys hardware, so you need a fast overcurrent trip.
Control, because converters use inductor current for current-mode control and motors produce torque proportional to current.
Monitoring, because integrating current gives battery state of charge and multiplying by voltage gives power. And diagnostics, like detecting a stalled motor or missing load.
The purpose sets the spec: protection wants speed, metering wants low offset, control wants bandwidth."
